title.narrative: Power of Pride Africa

description.narrative: Working towards diverse and inclusive societies in which LGBTI are able to participate to their full potential

"1. Individual LGBTI know and accept their SOGIESC and can ensure their rights in society are respected. They can meaningfully engage with societal structures. 2 A support system for LGBTI is developed based on discussionsabout common issues, needs and challenges, creating the motivationto act against discrimination and marginalisation. 3 LGBTI CBOs can strategically engage in societal and political decision-making processes using evidence-based advocacy. 4 Agile LGBTI movements are built that can work collectively to create social and political change and respond flexibly to various situations. 5 Institutions and other allies have an internal drive to includeLGBTI in their decision-making and other structures. LGBTI are actively engaged in processes and all policy-making spaces. 6 Strong and reliable laws and policies are in place for LGBTI and are enforced by all relevant bodies. Follow-up on these policies and their implementation are under scrutiny"

title.narrative: 11.2 Number of emergency cases supported.

description.narrative: This indicator accounts for the emergency cases supported

comment.narrative: Baseline was produce in collaboration with partners in country. Consultants typically had virtual meetings with members of the participatory grant making mechanism, or representatives of partners in the country. During these meetings consultants reflected together with the partners on how best to collect the baseline data and considered the different options for who could undertake the research. In some countries it was agreed that partners would directly collect the data and in other cases partners confirmed the appointment of or co-selected a researcher. Consultants contracted with relevant organisations or individuals in each country and ensured that they were briefed about the process, provided the organisations with the baseline template as well as the tools that had been developed and how best to administer them. The research in each country then took different forms including a desktop review, which included integrating data from the Country Context Analyses (CCA)and other relevant documents, facilitating focus groups (some hybrid) as well as individual interviews and surveys with each of the partners to collect qualitative data and quantitative data. Some countries also had interviews with allies. In addition, Consultants were able to administer survey to members of the LGBTI communities either directly at events or circulated via email, by partners or by the researchers. In total consultants received 162 partner responses and 1359 member responses to the surveys.
Targets were defined by baseline consultants following baseline numbers and percentages allocated per long term outcome in the years to come to calculate targets for the countries and overall program

In 2024, as state repression, anti-LGBTI legislation, and societal hostility intensified across several African countries, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) played a vital role—both directly and in partnership with community-based organisations—in supporting emergency response mechanisms for LGBTI individuals and activists. Recognising the increasingly precarious environment in which LGBTIQ+ people live and organise, PAI's interventions included direct support for digital and physical safety and capacity strengthening for grassroots actors navigating crisis scenarios. These interventions reflect PAI’s commitment not only to movement-building but also to ensuring the immediate protection and survival of the individuals who sustain those movements. Indirectly, PAI strengthened community resilience and emergency preparedness by equipping over 70 activists through regional Human Rights Mechanisms Trainings (HRMT) with tools to engage legal frameworks, seek protection, and understand redress mechanisms. While these trainings were not designed as emergency responses, their content proved critical in real-time scenarios where activists needed to navigate threats, claim legal standing, or seek international intervention. Similarly, PAI's participation in high-level policy spaces—such as the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights and the UN Human Rights Council—ensured that the persecution of LGBTI individuals in crisis contexts remained visible on international platforms, generating solidarity and accountability. PAI also recognised that emergency support goes beyond immediate safety—it is about preserving dignity, agency, and the right to exist in hostile environments. As such, safe spaces like the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, while not emergency interventions per se, served a protective function by offering temporary respite, healing, and strategizing space for leaders under immense pressure. These spaces became critical buffers against the burnout, trauma, and mental health crises that often follow emergency incidents.

In 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) transformed the landscape of LGBTI community engagement by establishing over ten safe, affirming spaces—both physical and virtual—that enabled over 100 activists to connect, heal, and act. These spaces did more than offer physical protection; they became catalytic environments for learning, self-acceptance, strategic collaboration, and collective resistance to marginalisation.Whether in retreat settings, human rights trainings, leadership forums, or digital convenings, each space served as a powerful incubator for political consciousness, psychosocial support, and sustained movement-building. These safe spaces, co-created with grassroots and feminist allies, were built on the foundation of shared lived experience, intersectional solidarity, and mutual accountability—allowing LGBTI individuals to gather around common challenges, define collective priorities, and emerge more resilient and mobilised to confront structural discrimination.A flagship initiative was the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, a physical safe space that convened 14 LGBTIQ+ leaders from across the country. Held from December 2–4, the retreat enabled critical dialogue on internal movement fragmentation, burnout, and power imbalances. Through a carefully facilitated process grounded in care, values clarification, and collective visioning, the retreat restored trust, deepened solidarity, and supported the development of a unified national advocacy direction. Beyond addressing individual wellbeing, it became a movement-strengthening intervention that is already generating ripple effects across Ghana's queer organising ecosystem.This was complemented by three Human Rights Mechanisms Trainings held across Ghana, Zimbabwe, and South Africa, reaching over 50 activists. These were not just technical trainings—they were safe, healing-centred environments where participants could speak freely, support one another, and build strategic power. The Southern Africa sessions, in particular, incorporated trauma-informed methodologies and peer-led facilitation, creating space for healing, skills development, and identity affirmation. These gatherings fostered lasting peer networks, reinforced regional solidarity, and gave participants the tools—and confidence—to engage with regional and international human rights mechanisms.The Leadership Development Forum, held in Johannesburg in June 2024, brought together 16 leaders from LGBTIQ+ organisations across the continent. The fconvening combined sessions on governance and organisational sustainability with intentional spaces for personal reflection, mutual support, and solidarity building. Participants reported increased leadership confidence, renewed motivation, and an expanded network of peers. The forum served as a safe incubator for sharing lived experiences and navigating the complexities of leading queer organisations in often-hostile national contexts.In the feminist space, PAI co-convened the Feminist Solidarity Convening in Ghana, organised by Courageous Sisters Ghana. With diverse feminist actors and LBQT persons in the room, the convening provided an affirming and political space where participants deepened their understanding of international human rights frameworks such as CEDAW. Through facilitated sessions on collective action and joint advocacy planning, participants established a stronger sense of inter-movement solidarity, and some began building cross-sector collaborations that continue to take root. This safe space explicitly acknowledged and addressed the unique forms of marginalisation LBQT persons face within feminist spaces, making it a vital corrective and bridge-building moment.In the virtual space, PAI supported ongoing digital engagements , using platforms such as webinars, virtual dialogues, and strategy meetings. These digital safe spaces proved especially vital for activists in countries with high levels of surveillance, legal repression, or insecurity. PAI’s virtual programming ensured continued access to information, peer solidarity, and emotional support—especially for those unable to travel or who faced criminalisation in their home countries. One standout example was the Activist Soirée hosted during the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF), which created a space for reflection, emotional connection, and strategising among activists who had participated in global development advocacy. The Soirée created a rare opportunity for personal grounding and peer validation in the midst of high-pressure global advocacy work.Outcomes Achieved:Over 100 LGBTIQ+ individuals participated in at least 10 structured safe spaces (6 physical and 4 virtual) across the continent in 2024.These spaces addressed individual and collective trauma, created opportunities for emotional and strategic alignment, and deepened intra- and inter-movement solidarity.Participants gained increased confidence, political agency, and a sense of belonging, often for the first time in formalised activist settings.Several of these convenings led to follow-up collaborations, joint advocacy initiatives, and national or regional strategy development, showing that these spaces were not one-off interventions but springboards for deeper structural organising.Digital safe spaces extended the reach and accessibility of PAI’s programming, ensuring sustained contact and care-based communication between activists across contexts of isolation or legal insecurity.PAI has directly responded to the need for community-based support systems that reinforce resilience, acceptance, and advocacy. These spaces are not neutral containers—they are sites of resistance, repair, and reimagination. They enable LGBTI people to stand taller, speak louder, and stay connected—turning isolation into collective power. In the face of growing anti-rights backlash, PAI’s safe spaces are not just reactive—they are transformative.

In 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) made substantial progress in strengthening the advocacy capacity of LGBTI grassroots organisations, CBOs, and CSOs, directly contributing to actions aimed at influencing laws, policies, and societal norms across Africa. Through strategic support, capacity-building initiatives, and collaborative platforms, PAI has enabled partners and activists to carry out advocacy initiatives that challenge hostile environments and promote inclusion.Key Results:•Expansion of Advocacy at Regional Mechanisms:PAI facilitated the participation of 12 activists at the 81st Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, enabling them to directly engage with Commissioners, deliver statements, and advocate for LGBTIQ+ rights on the 10th anniversary of Resolution 275. This engagement strengthened activists' capacities to influence regional human rights discourse and encouraged broader recognition of SOGIESC rights across Africa.•National-Level Advocacy for Systemic Change:Through the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, PAI created a platform for 14 movement leaders to assess systemic barriers, collectively strategise, and commit to advancing advocacy initiatives in response to the Ghanaian anti-LGBTIQ+ bill. Leaders committed to building a unified movement that would influence societal norms by fostering shared values, organising around common goals, and improving collaboration mechanisms. This repositioning laid the foundation for a coordinated national advocacy agenda.•Evidence-Based Advocacy at Global Platforms:PAI supported Ugandan and South African activists in developing spotlight reports for the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF), which were used to advocate for the inclusion of LGBTIQ+ issues in national SDG discussions. By linking local evidence to global frameworks, activists were able to directly inform and influence policy narratives around sustainable development and human rights.•Advocacy through Strategic Reports to Human Rights Bodies:PAI provided technical and financial support for the submission of Universal Periodic Review (UPR) stakeholder reports for Egypt and Ivory Coast. These reports highlighted systemic discrimination against LGBTIQ+ individuals and served as critical advocacy tools to hold governments accountable at the UN Human Rights Council.•Regional Strategy Development to Sustain Advocacy:During the South Africa Human Rights Activists Forum, PAI and partners collaboratively developed a shared regional advocacy strategy. This collective plan, developed through participatory engagement with grassroots activists and CSOs, will serve as a roadmap for influencing legal reforms and challenging anti-rights narratives across Southern Africa.Outcomes Achieved:•Increased engagement of grassroots activists in regional and international advocacy spaces.•Strengthened cross-movement alliances and formulation of shared advocacy strategies at national and regional levels.•Amplified LGBTIQ+ voices in high-level human rights discussions, increasing visibility and political pressure on governments.•Fostered a shift towards evidence-driven advocacy, equipping grassroots movements with data and narratives to influence laws and norms.•Initiated processes for movement governance reforms and national advocacy frameworks to ensure sustainability beyond ad hoc initiatives.Conclusion:Through deliberate and sustained interventions in 2024, PAI has not only catalysed new advocacy initiatives led by grassroots and community organisations but has also embedded a culture of strategic, evidence-based, and collective action. These efforts are progressively influencing legal frameworks, reshaping societal narratives, and building the political power of LGBTIQ+ communities across Africa. PAI’s participatory, feminist, and Global South-rooted approach ensures that those most impacted by discrimination are positioned as key agents of change in advocacy processes.

Throughout 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) has significantly contributed to strengthening partnerships and fostering alliances that work towards collectively formulated strategies, both within the LGBTIQ+ movement and across broader human rights spaces. Recognising that intersectionality and collective organising are critical for sustainable change, PAI actively facilitated cross-organisational collaborations, movement-wide dialogues, and joint strategy development across local, regional, and continental levels.At the national level, in response to the increasingly hostile environment in Ghana following the passage of the anti-LGBTIQ+ bill, PAI convened the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat (December 2024).This retreat brought together 14 key leaders from grassroots organisations, CBOs, and CSOs to assess the state of the LGBTIQ+ movement, rebuild trust, and co-create a shared vision for advocacy. Through facilitated dialogues, participants engaged in mapping systemic barriers, addressing fragmentation, and collectively redefining the priorities and values of the movement. This process led to tangible next steps, such as establishing a working group, drafting governance frameworks, and setting plans for a national movement fund—all rooted in a collectively developed agenda. This represents a critical example of PAI's role in deepening alliances based on joint strategic frameworks responding to shared injustices.At the regional level, PAI’s participation in the South Africa Human Rights Activists Forum, convened by SALC and GALZ, further demonstrated its commitment to cross-movement collaboration​. Here, activists and civil society leaders across Southern Africa developed a shared regional strategy to address systemic discrimination against LGBTIQ+ persons. PAI’s contributions helped facilitate the formulation of a collective advocacy roadmap for the region, reinforcing the importance of sustained, intersectional, and coordinated action.Additionally, PAI’s leadership in the 81st Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights built new alliances among LGBTIQ+ activists engaging with human rights mechanisms​. By supporting 12 activists to participate and advocate collectively around the 10th anniversary of Resolution 275, PAI fostered a space where joint advocacy strategies could be formulated, strengthening the movement’s regional voice.Through these efforts, PAI did not only focus on partnerships within the LGBTIQ+ movement but also reached across movements by working alongside feminist groups (e.g., through the Ghana feminist solidarity convening), human rights defenders at the African Commission, and development actors engaging with Sustainable Development Goals at the High-Level Political Forum​. This cross-sectoral approach helped align LGBTIQ+ advocacy with broader struggles for human rights, democracy, and gender justice. In all these initiatives, PAI emphasised participatory approaches grounded in feminist and Global South perspectives—centring the voices of marginalised communities in setting agendas, defining advocacy priorities, and collectively determining strategies. This has not only strengthened the resilience of the LGBTIQ+ movement but has also contributed to building a more unified, intersectional, and strategic front capable of confronting rising anti-rights movements across Africa.

Grounding Advocacy in Evidence, Accountability, and Community VoiceIn a year marked by heightened repression and shrinking civic space, LGBTI grassroots organisations across Africa have continued to emerge as credible, accountable, and strategic advocates—not only of their own rights, but also within broader human rights and development discourses. In 2024, PAI accelerated efforts to equip these organisations with the knowledge, tools, and evidence they need to lead sustainable and representative lobbying and advocacy (L&A) initiatives.Through a combination of participatory research, advocacy strategy development, stakeholder reporting, and high-level engagement, PAI supported at least nine (9) LGBTI grassroots organisations and CBOs to deepen their engagement with national, regional, and global policy platforms. These interventions not only strengthened the capacity of CBOs to build and use evidence but also reinforced their ability to operate with community legitimacy, internal accountability, and clear mandates.As part of this, PAI supported the development and submission of two Universal Periodic Review (UPR) stakeholder reports in Egypt and Ivory Coast. These reports, developed through community-driven research and consultation, documented structural human rights violations affecting marginalised populations—including women and gender-diverse persons—and brought them to the attention of the UN Human Rights Council. Over 20 activists were supported in the process, improving their capacity to collect data, frame rights-based recommendations, and engage with international review mechanisms.PAI also facilitated the development of two national Spotlight Reports (Uganda and South Africa), presented at the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF). These reports critically assessed national progress on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), using a gender-inclusive development lens. Through participatory validation and advocacy preparation, CBOs built their capacity to gather evidence, formulate policy messages, and engage in multilateral advocacy rooted in the lived realities of their communities.Beyond written outputs, PAI directly invested in strengthening advocacy strategy skills through three Human Rights Mechanisms Trainings (HRMTs). These trainings focused on practical skills for engaging with regional and international mechanisms, including the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, CEDAW, and UN Special Procedures. Participants developed advocacy action plans linked to institutional mandates and community needs, reinforcing both internal planning and external influence.PAI’s participation in the Summit of the Future created additional opportunities to integrate LGBTIQ+ and gender-inclusive development perspectives into global governance discussions. Through networking, message coordination, and informal strategy support, PAI contributed to preparing grassroots partners to engage in these spaces with clarity and purpose—expanding their confidence and visibility on global platforms.In Ghana, the Movement Leaders Retreat provided space for grassroots organisations to reflect on the state of the movement and strengthen the alignment between their advocacy priorities and their organisational values. Several organisations used this opportunity to refine their mandates, internal advocacy strategies, and recommit to representing their communities with transparency and accountability. Finally, through the Leadership Forum, PAI trained 16 leaders from LGBTI CBOs across the continent in strategic advocacy planning, aligning mission statements with programmatic L&A, and embedding evidence and values into external engagement.Through these interventions, PAI ensured that LGBTI CBOs are not only visible in high-level spaces but also prepared, resourced, and accountable in their advocacy efforts. By building evidence, developing advocacy strategies, and connecting organisational mandates to community priorities, these CBOs are now leading sustainable, legitimate, and representative L&A efforts across Africa and beyond.

In 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI), under the Power of Pride (PoP) programme, supported a diverse and growing network of civil society organisations (CSOs), CBOs, and grassroots groups committed to advancing LGBTIQ+ rights, gender equality, and inclusive development across Africa. This support extended beyond formal contractual partnerships to include a wider cohort of organisations that benefited from technical assistance, capacity development, participation in events, and collaboration in joint advocacy and learning interventions.Over the reporting period, PAI supported CSOs and CBOs through a combination of direct partnership, co-implementation, training, and movement-building platforms. These were mostly engaged through non contractual arrangements. These organisations led on-the-ground interventions related to advocacy, capacity building, civic space defence, and regional human rights engagement. These organisations took part in a range of initiatives, including the Leadership Development Forum, the Human Rights Mechanisms Trainings (HRMTs), the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, the Feminist Solidarity Convening, and global advocacy engagements such as the High-Level Political Forum and Summit of the Future. These engagements focused on strengthening advocacy strategy, organisational development, intersectional movement building, and engagement with regional and international human rights mechanisms. In several instances, CSOs that were not formal PoP grantees became part of the broader ecosystem of support—co-authoring reports, co-facilitating convenings, or cascading knowledge within their local communities. This participatory and decentralised approach allowed PAI to extend the reach and impact of the PoP programme beyond its immediate member portfolio. PAI also worked through regional civil society platforms such as the ACSE Strategy Validation Meeting, which brought together organisations from across the continent to develop a unified advocacy framework for engagement with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights. These convenings created space for newer or emerging organisations—particularly grassroots and under-resourced actors—to gain visibility, forge alliances, and contribute meaningfully to continental strategy.Through this layered and inclusive approach, PAI has demonstrated that sustainable movement-building extends beyond contracts—it requires accessible platforms, trusted relationships, and collaborative learning environments. The growing ecosystem of CSOs supported under PoP now reflects a broader base of organisations equipped with the skills, solidarity, and strategic clarity to push for meaningful change at all levels.

Throughout 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) actively supported LGBTI grassroots organisations and CBOs to strengthen their financial sustainability as a foundation for independent, accountable, and legitimate community representation. Recognising that financial vulnerability undermines both credibility and continuity, PAI worked to build the capacities of CBOs to mobilise resources, diversify funding streams, and develop proposals aligned with their mandates and community needs.PAI supported at least 10 grassroots CBOs and CSOs across various regions in Africa to enhance their financial management and fundraising capabilities. These interventions were integrated into broader organisational development efforts that aimed to improve institutional sustainability, community accountability, and programmatic coherence. The sessions focused on proposal developments, donor mapping, and resource mobilisation strategies, helping organisations shift from reactive funding models to proactive, mission-driven financial planning. Components of this work were embedded within the Leadership Forum, where 16 LGBTI organisational leaders received training on financial planning, donor engagement, and risk-informed sustainability strategies. Participants reported increased confidence in aligning their funding proposals with their organisational vision and in setting up basic internal financial control systems to improve accountability to both donors and communities they serve.PAI also facilitated discussions on alternative funding models, including community-based fundraising, strategic partnerships, and pooled movement funds. During the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, participating CBOs explored the development of a dedicated movement fund, grounded in mutual accountability and shared values. As a result, several CBOs committed to piloting small-scale community contribution systems to reduce over-reliance on external donors and foster local ownership.In addition, PAI’s technical accompaniment in advocacy-related processes—such as the development of Spotlight Reports and regional strategy frameworks—helped several organisations position themselves for new funding opportunities by demonstrating alignment with broader human rights and sustainable development agendas. This strategic positioning not only enhances their visibility to donors but also contributes to their long-term legitimacy as actors capable of influencing systems change.

2024 saw Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) investing in strengthening the internal capacities of LGBTI community-based organisations (CBOs) to ensure they operate with clarity of purpose, organisational accountability, and community legitimacy. Recognising that effective representation requires more than visibility, PAI supported grassroots CBOs to develop foundational skills in leadership, governance, administration, and planning processes—thereby enhancing their credibility and ability to respond to the needs of their constituencies in a transparent and sustainable manner.Through a combination of leadership forums, movement retreats, technical facilitation, and peer learning sessions, PAI supported at least 15 LGBTI CBOs and grassroots organisations across Africa to strengthen their internal systems and structures. This included support for the development and revision of organisational mandates, creation or improvement of codes of conduct, and training on decision-making frameworks, enabling organisations to articulate their mission more clearly and practice inclusive governance.A key moment in this work was the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, where Movement leaders engaged in intensive reflection on organisational fragmentation and movement cohesion. Through facilitated sessions on governance frameworks and shared values, several participating CBOs committed to redefining their mandates and developing clear internal decision-making processes. This included setting up or refining their internal accountability mechanisms to ensure alignment with community priorities, as well as establishing systems for reporting, feedback, and ethical leadership.In addition, PAI convened a Leadership Forum that brought together 16 organisational leaders for a programme focused on adaptive leadership, sustainability planning, and strategic governance. Participants reported a stronger understanding of their roles in community accountability and left with actionable plans to strengthen financial transparency, board engagement, and programmatic oversight in their respective organisations.PAI also provided technical support and coaching in the context of regional strategy processes, including the ACSE Strategy Validation Meeting, where participating CBOs were guided in aligning their organisational strategies with broader human rights mechanisms. Amidst intensifying anti-rights backlash across Africa and globally, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) and its members made strategic gains in securing state commitments to inclusive language, policies, and frameworks that affirm the rights of LGBTIQ+ communities. Through coordinated advocacy, technical support, and engagement at multiple governance levels, PAI contributed to the adoption of recommendations, resolutions, and declarations that embed SOGIESC concerns within national, regional, and global policy processes.PAI supported the development and submission of two Universal Periodic Review (UPR) stakeholder reports—in Egypt and Ivory Coast—which highlighted systemic exclusion and rights violations faced by marginalised communities. These efforts led to three (3) recommendations accepted by states, referencing non-discrimination, equality, and legal protections—marking critical, state-endorsed entry points for ongoing accountability.Additionally, two Spotlight Reports—from Uganda and South Africa—were presented at the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) and played a key role in reinforcing the retention of inclusive language such as “leaving no one behind” and “gender equality” in the Forum’s final declarations. These contributions demonstrated the power of evidence-based advocacy in shaping global development commitments.PAI’s advocacy extended to the Summit of the Future, where it collaborated with global allies to resist coordinated anti-rights efforts and successfully protect inclusive and rights-affirming language within outcome documents adopted by member states.Regionally, PAI deepened its engagement with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) by supporting 12 activists to participate in the 81st Ordinary Session, including pre-sessions and commemorative events marking the 10th anniversary of Resolution 275. Civil society interventions during the session reaffirmed the need for implementation of existing protections, culminating in a public acknowledgement by the ACHPR Chair of ongoing LGBTIQ+ rights violations across the continent. This marked a notable shift in institutional visibility and state-facing accountability on SOGIESC issues.Further strategic alignment was achieved through the ACSE Strategy Validation Meeting, where PAI helped shape a regional advocacy roadmap linking national-level demands with ACHPR commitments—ensuring continuity in follow-up efforts and alignment with inclusive human rights standards.In parallel, activists supported by PAI issued public statements at both the UN and African Commission forums, reinforcing the legitimacy of inclusive legal language and applying public pressure on states to uphold their human rights obligations. These interventions translated into tangible advocacy wins, ensuring that inclusive terminology and state commitments were not only adopted but also positioned for implementation and monitoring. Through this integrated, multi-tiered advocacy, PAI ensured that inclusive laws and policies are not only preserved in principle but also adopted in practice—anchoring future enforcement and accountability within a strong rights-based framework.

In a year marked by escalating anti-rights agendas and legislative attacks on LGBTI communities across Africa, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) and its members played a pivotal role in efforts to block or stall the progression of harmful laws and prevent the dilution of inclusive language at both national and international levels. Through coordinated civil society pressure, diplomatic engagement, and strategic participation in international forums, PAI contributed to actions that prevented the adoption or implementation of policies that would have further restricted the rights, freedoms, and recognition of LGBTI people.During 2024, at least two (2) harmful legal or policy actions were successfully blocked or stalled as a direct result of civil society mobilisation, in which PAI played a contributing role through technical support, coordination, or advocacy amplification.In Ghana, following the passage of the anti-LGBTIQ+ bill in Parliament in February 2024, PAI collaborated with national organisations to mobilise diplomatic pressure and international visibility that significantly delayed the bill's progression into law. Although passed by Parliament, the bill has not been signed into law by the President, partly due to sustained civil society advocacy, international engagement, and the active involvement of diplomatic missions. PAI’s role included facilitating advocacy briefings, amplifying activist voices through regional and global platforms, and supporting the development of messaging that framed the bill as a violation of democratic principles, human rights obligations, and constitutional protections.At the international level, PAI and other members of the Power of Pride alliance actively participated in regional and global advocacy spaces, including the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF) and the Summit of the Future, where civil society successfully resisted attempts to erase or dilute inclusive language related to sexual orientation, gender identity, and bodily autonomy from policy outcome documents. In particular, coordinated pressure from African and global South civil society groups—including messaging developed with PAI’s support—helped ensure that gender-inclusive and rights-affirming language was retained in key negotiations, especially within SDG and multilateral governance frameworks.These outcomes were achieved not through isolated campaigns but through coordinated advocacy strategies, strong ally engagement (including with diplomatic missions), and the use of evidence-based narratives and legal arguments—strengthened by PAI’s regional reach and strategic positioning. In both national and international spaces, PAI’s involvement helped ensure that harmful legal and rhetorical shifts were either stalled, reframed, or blocked altogether, demonstrating the power of informed and collective resistance.These results underscore the strategic role civil society—and particularly LGBTI-led organisations—can play in resisting regressive policy shifts. Through sustained advocacy, alliance-building, and rights-based framing, PAI has helped prevent additional legal harm and ensured that inclusive language continues to serve as a normative anchor in global governance and development frameworks.

Despite a context marked by rising anti-rights narratives, conservative legislation, and shrinking civic space across much of Africa, 2024 witnessed strategic openings where civil society, including Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) and its members, contributed to the adoption, improvement, or implementation of inclusive laws, policies, and normative frameworks. These wins—though emerging in a complex and often regressive environment—reflect the continued commitment and resilience of LGBTI movements in advancing SOGIESC rights through legal, institutional, and discursive change.During the year, two significant policy or normative shifts were recorded where inclusive frameworks were advanced or adopted with direct or indirect contributions from PAI and its allies.In Namibia, civil society, supported through regional advocacy momentum and visibility—including contributions from PAI—welcomed the landmark ruling by the Supreme Court that recognised same-sex marriages contracted abroad. This decision marked a historic precedent in a region where legal recognition of same-sex relationships remains rare. Although backlash followed in the form of counter-legislation, the initial ruling remains a powerful legal milestone that formalised recognition of same-sex couples in specific legal contexts. PAI supported regional members to amplify the ruling’s significance and to use it as an advocacy tool for movement-building and public education around constitutional protections and international human rights law.In Kenya, ongoing legal advocacy and public campaigning by movement actors, including PoP-supported organisations, resulted in the affirmation of the right of association for LGBTIQ+ groups by the Supreme Court. This ruling upheld that denying registration to organisations on the basis of sexual orientation was unconstitutional. PAI provided strategic communications support and contributed to broader regional solidarity campaigns that helped frame the ruling within a broader context of civic space and equality rights. While the ruling faced political backlash, it represents a major normative shift toward state-level recognition of LGBTIQ+ civil society as legitimate actors.In addition to these legal rulings, PAI and members contributed to shifting norms within African regional and global governance frameworks by defending and promoting inclusive language in multilateral policy documents. For example, during the High-Level Political Forum and the Summit of the Future, inclusive references to gender, diversity, and non-discrimination were maintained despite coordinated anti-rights efforts to weaken them. PAI’s behind-the-scenes support in shaping advocacy messaging, amplifying African voices, and engaging diplomatic allies was instrumental in ensuring that normative frameworks within the UN system continued to reflect principles of inclusion and universality.The operating environment in 2024, however, remained deeply polarised. The advancement of anti-LGBTI legislation in Ghana, Mali, Liberia, and Burkina Faso—as well as disinformation campaigns across Cameroon, Malawi, and Côte d’Ivoire—has significantly worsened the legal and social climate for LGBTI communities. Yet even in this context, the ability to secure progressive court rulings, uphold inclusive legal interpretations, and resist the removal of inclusive language from global policy spaces demonstrates the resilience and strategic sophistication of LGBTI advocacy actors across the continent.These policy and normative wins, while occurring amidst a hostile regional landscape, are critical building blocks toward the realisation of inclusive and diverse societies. By embedding SOGIESC principles in law and institutional language, PAI and its members have helped protect space for ongoing advocacy, affirmed the legitimacy of LGBTI communities, and signaled to governments and international actors alike that progress is possible—even when the political winds are against it.

In 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) strategically supported grassroots organisations, CBOs, and CSOs across Africa to carry out actions that directly and indirectly contributed to raising awareness and fostering acceptance within LGBTI communities. Through targeted capacity-building, leadership development, feminist convenings, and strategic advocacy engagements, PAI worked to ensure that LGBTI individuals had access to knowledge, tools, and supportive spaces that enabled self-acceptance, legal awareness, and meaningful engagement with societal structures.One of the central components of this work was the Human Rights Mechanisms Trainings in Ghana and Southern Africa. In Ghana, 20 activists were equipped with practical knowledge and skills on engaging international and regional human rights systems. This not only expanded their understanding of their legal rights and protections but also built their confidence to advocate for themselves and their communities. Similarly, trainings in Southern Africa empowered over 30 activists from Zimbabwe, Zambia, and South Africa with advocacy tools grounded in human rights frameworks. Beyond skill-building, these sessions fostered solidarity, strengthened political consciousness, and cultivated pride in identity among LGBTI activists.Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat further advanced internal community awareness and collective healing. Bringing together 14 movement leaders, the retreat created space for reflection on movement challenges, values clarification, and power dynamics. The dialogue fostered renewed commitment to shared goals and inclusion within the movement, reinforcing internal cohesion and promoting self-acceptance at individual and collective levels.A notable contribution to feminist-led community consciousness-raising was the Feminist Solidarity Convening in Ghana, organized by Courageous Sisters Ghana. PAI's Advocacy Manager facilitated a session on leveraging the CEDAW framework to advance LBQT rights. This convening strengthened feminist alliances and expanded knowledge-sharing on international human rights frameworks among feminist groups. Observable results included follow-up advocacy plans and collaborative initiatives. More significantly, the convening likely catalyzed shifts in understanding and attitudes towards collective feminist action, especially among participants engaging with SOGIESC issues for the first time.In line with promoting evidence-based self-advocacy, PAI supported the development and dissemination of Spotlight Reports in Uganda and South Africa. The participatory development of these reports enabled LGBTI individuals to critically reflect on how SDGs intersect with their lived realities. Activists who presented these reports at the High-Level Political Forum experienced a boost in confidence and political agency, as they saw their local issues being spotlighted on a global platform.Similarly, PAI facilitated the production of UPR Stakeholder Reports in Egypt and Ivory Coast. These processes helped grassroots activists document systemic violations, claim visibility, and understand mechanisms of international accountability. In both countries, the process of creating these reports increased legal literacy and encouraged a sense of self-worth and empowerment among community members, particularly in contexts where state repression has historically silenced LGBTI voices.PAI’s work at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the South Africa Human Rights Activists Forum, and the Summit of the Future created further visibility and engagement opportunities for LGBTI individuals to be recognised in regional and global policy discourse. These engagements served not only external advocacy goals but also sent a strong internal message to LGBTI communities across Africa: that their presence, perspectives, and rights matter—and that they have a place in shaping the continent’s political future.Outcomes Achieved:Increased access to information on SOGIESC, legal rights, and human rights frameworks for LGBTI communities.Strengthened self-esteem, identity pride, and collective political consciousness among grassroots activists and community members.Fostered internal solidarity, dialogue, and trust-building among LGBTI leaders, collectives, and feminist allies.Expanded capacity to meaningfully engage with societal and policy structures at local, regional, and global levels.Reinforced intersectional, feminist, and decolonial approaches to community empowerment and movement-building.By supporting these interconnected initiatives, PAI has helped shape a more informed, empowered, and cohesive LGBTI community across Africa. These efforts not only raise awareness but also deepen internal acceptance and agency, ensuring that LGBTI individuals are equipped not only to survive—but to thrive—as active participants in reshaping the societies they live in.

In response to increasing threats to civic space across Africa, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) worked in 2024 to support grassroots organisations, CBOs, and CSOs in advancing actions aimed at protecting and expanding their operational freedom, legal recognition, and ability to perform critical advocacy, organising, and service delivery functions. These actions were particularly vital in countries where governments have weaponised laws, bureaucratic hurdles, and moral panic to restrict the functioning of LGBTI and human rights organisations.Over the past year, PAI and its partners undertook at least six (6) documented actions across five countries to influence civic space in ways that enable greater participation, legitimacy, and institutional protection for grassroots actors.In Ghana, where civic space has rapidly deteriorated due to the passage of the anti-LGBTIQ+ bill in Parliament, grassroots leaders engaged in multiple advocacy and dialogue efforts with diplomatic actors and civil society coalitions to raise awareness on the bill’s chilling effect on freedom of association and NGO registration. As part of this effort, PAI supported organisations in documenting civic threats, conducting community-level dialogue, and contributing to consultations with two diplomatic missions, calling for international solidarity and support for protective mechanisms. While full reversal of the bill remains pending, these engagements strengthened visibility and built political pressure that has prevented full-scale implementation to date.In Egypt and Ivory Coast, PAI supported grassroots organisations to develop and submit two UPR stakeholder reports that highlighted state-imposed restrictions on NGO operations, funding barriers, and surveillance of human rights actors. These reports were used to call for state compliance with international obligations on freedom of assembly and association. Beyond the reports themselves, the process contributed to community capacity-building around strategic rights-based advocacy, giving CBOs tools to engage with government and UN mechanisms on civic space issues. Through its participation in the ACSE Strategy Validation Meeting, PAI further supported the finalisation of a regional civil society engagement roadmap with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR). The strategy included explicit recommendations on addressing shrinking civic space and the protection of defenders, particularly in contexts where states are pushing repressive NGO legislation or blocking registration of LGBTI and feminist organisations.Additionally, several CBOs participating in the Leadership Forum and Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat used these platforms to articulate collective responses to increasing restrictions—mapping power, planning response strategies, and identifying protection pathways to safeguard their continued operation. These discussions laid the groundwork for future coalition-building and advocacy campaigns to counter registration denials, police harassment, and bureaucratic delays. PAI’s presence at the Summit of the Future also created an opportunity to insert African civil society perspectives into global governance dialogues, helping ensure that the importance of civic space—particularly for LGBTI and feminist movements in the Global South—was acknowledged at the highest levels. By amplifying civic space concerns through formal reporting, direct advocacy, and strategic convening, PAI has ensured that the closing of space for LGBTI and human rights organisations in Africa is met with informed, coordinated, and community-led responses. These actions continue to lay the foundation for a more enabling environment where grassroots voices can organise, advocate, and thrive without fear.

Partners carried out many different forms of advocacy on a national level, towards provincial governments, national ministries and societal actors, government institutions and societal actors. Whilst most partners engaged in advocacy regarding better access to services such as healthcare and education, mentioned under ‘mobilising allies’ – essential lobbying actions were undertaken in tow of our country partners, in direct response to the negative threats to the legal space. This included the fight against anti-LGBTI legislation and the involvment of UN agencies, as well as a Dutch embassy. Regional advocacy work took place at the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), the African Union (AU) and the Treaty Monitoring Body (TMB) at the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD), which is a part of the UN. In October/November 2021, PAI conducted a human rights and international advocacy training, for the countries who were up for review at the ACHPR at the time. 31 participants from 13 different countries were equipped with practical knowledge and training on how to effectively engage the ACHPR, as well as their own states and government. During this training, PAI facilitated the development of country-specific advocacy strategies, as well as the development of a collective regional strategic on SOGIESC. These strategies include engagements before, during and after the official review. ILGA Asia supported a young transgender activist in November 2021. This activist was able to join a mission in Geneva and engage with members of the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. She held 5 meetings with the CERD committee members, the French Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Federation for Human Rights members, and officials from the OHCHR in Geneva. Globally, there were many, many opportunities to engage in human rights and policy spaces. Due to the sheer number of these, Power of Pride prioritised the Human Rights Council (HRC), the Universal Periodic Reviews (UPRs) the UN High Level Political Forum (HLPF), the UN Commission on the Status of Women (CSW).

Throughout 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) significantly strengthened its role in amplifying LGBTIQ+ voices and advancing broader human rights and gender-inclusive development frameworks by supporting the development, drafting, and submission of key statements, shadow reports, and advocacy documents. These initiatives provided vital evidence for international, regional, and national mechanisms, embedding LGBTIQ+ concerns within wider human rights, SRHR, and sustainable development discussions.In the past year, PAI directly contributed to at least six (6) major reports and statements that addressed both specific LGBTIQ+ rights issues and broader frameworks of human rights, gender equality, and inclusive development.A critical contribution was the support provided for the development and submission of two (2) UPR stakeholder reports: One for Egypt, where PAI provided technical and financial assistance to local activists to document systemic rights violations and advocate for legal reforms through the Universal Periodic Review process.Another for Ivory Coast, marking the first-ever LGBTIQ-specific stakeholder report submitted from the country to the Human Rights Council​. Through technical coaching and capacity-building, PAI enabled over 20 activists to successfully engage with this critical accountability process, thus advancing not only LGBTIQ+ rights but also broader human rights norms related to non-discrimination, access to health, and legal recognition.In the context of gender-inclusive development, PAI supported the production of two (2) national Spotlight Reports for the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF):One in Uganda and one in South Africa, developed through participatory validation processes involving grassroots activists​. These reports critically assessed the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) from an LGBTIQ+ and broader human rights lens, highlighting intersections between discrimination, poverty, health, and education. The reports were presented at the HLPF in New York, ensuring that gender-diverse voices were integrated into global sustainable development dialogues. By centring the lived realities of marginalised populations, these reports advanced inclusive development priorities beyond traditional SRHR frameworks.PAI also contributed technical expertise and support toward the regional ACSE Strategy Validation, which produced a collective civil society strategic document guiding LGBTI and broader human rights engagement with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR). Although technically a strategic framework rather than a shadow report, it represents a key collective advocacy document designed to strengthen civil society’s influence on human rights jurisprudence across Africa, including on gender and SOGIESC rights.Additionally, PAI’s Advocacy Manager played a leading facilitation role in the Feminist Solidarity Convening in Ghana, where CEDAW-based advocacy strategies for LBQT persons were discussed and strengthened​. While no formal shadow report was produced during the convening itself, the convening contributed to growing capacities for future submissions to bodies such as the CEDAW Committee, ensuring that gender-inclusive development and intersectional feminist advocacy are embedded in future reporting cycles.By embedding LGBTIQ+ and feminist perspectives into global, regional, and national human rights instruments, PAI has ensured that advocacy efforts are intersectional, inclusive, and transformative. These efforts not only amplified marginalised voices in policy spaces but also strengthened the strategic positioning of LGBTIQ+ communities within broader human rights and sustainable development movements.

Some countries also had interviews with allies. In addition, Consultants were able to administer survey to members of the LGBTI communities either directly at events or circulated via email, by partners or by the researchers. In 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) actively supported the integration of feminist, gender-inclusive, and broader human rights priorities into regional and international policy spaces by contributing to the drafting, development, and validation of key reports, statements, and strategic advocacy documents. Through technical coaching, facilitation, and collaboration with activists and civil society organisations (CSOs), PAI helped ensure that intersectional human rights concerns—particularly those affecting womxn, girls, and marginalised communities—were amplified and included in critical human rights and development processes.Over the reporting period, PAI substantively contributed to three (3) key advocacy outputs aligned with broader human rights and gender-inclusive development frameworks:Spotlight Report on Uganda (High-Level Political Forum, HLPF)-PAI provided technical advocacy coaching and resource support for the development of a Spotlight Report assessing Uganda’s progress on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) from a gender-inclusive development perspective.This report documented barriers to access to health, education, and social protection services faced by marginalised communities, including women and girls, within the SDG implementation process. It advanced broader development goals by highlighting structural inequalities without focusing solely on LGBTIQ+ issues.Spotlight Report on South Africa (High-Level Political Forum, HLPF)-Similarly, PAI supported the development and validation of a Spotlight Report for South Africa, focused on sustainable development, social inclusion, gender equity, and human rights challenges. The report was presented during the HLPF, contributing to shaping discussions on inclusive development and the need for gender-responsive accountability in SDG implementation.Regional Civil Society Strategy (ACSE Strategy Validation Meeting)-PAI provided technical support and participated in the finalisation of a regional civil society strategy developed through the African Civil Society Engagement (ACSE) platform. This strategic document guides CSO advocacy towards the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) with an emphasis on broader human rights frameworks, regional development challenges, state accountability, and gender equity. It was built through multi-stakeholder input, and its validation strengthened regional advocacy coherence on gender, human rights, and participatory governance beyond LGBTIQ-specific concerns.In addition to these tangible outputs, PAI’s participation in spaces like the Feminist Solidarity Convening in Ghana further contributed to enhancing activists’ ability to use broader frameworks, such as CEDAW, for advancing gender-inclusive development and human rights advocacy. While this convening did not produce a formal shadow report, it directly contributed to strengthening technical competencies for future engagement with treaty bodies and gender accountability processes.

In 2024, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) strategically strengthened the capacity of LGBTI grassroots organisations, CBOs, and CSOs to design and implement advocacy initiatives aimed at influencing laws, policies, and societal norms across Africa. Through a combination of capacity building, alliance strengthening, strategic convenings, and evidence-based advocacy, PAI enabled activists and organisations to undertake coordinated actions that informed, educated, and engaged decision-makers capable of shifting societal and legal frameworks.A key highlight of the year was PAI’s facilitation of the participation of twelve activists at the 81st Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights. Through technical support and strategic accompaniment, activists engaged in pre-sessions, delivered statements, and participated in commemorations of the 10th anniversary of Resolution 275, helping to center SOGIESC rights within regional human rights dialogues. This contributed to expanding grassroots-led advocacy at a continental level, enhancing visibility for LGBTIQ+ rights within influential spaces.Complementing this, PAI played a leading role in the African Civil Society Engagement (ACSE) Strategy Validation Meeting. This forum brought together key regional CSOs and activists to finalize a coordinated strategy for engaging with the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights. By contributing to the shaping and validation of this collective advocacy roadmap, PAI directly strengthened regional civil society’s ability to engage systematically with regional human rights mechanisms and influence legal and policy frameworks affecting LGBTIQ+ persons.At the national level, PAI convened the Ghana Movement Leaders Retreat, providing a critical space for fourteen movement leaders to collectively reflect on the fragmentation within the Ghanaian movement and to redefine their shared vision, goals, and values. Emerging from the retreat was a clear commitment to rebuilding a unified, coordinated movement capable of resisting the anti-LGBTIQ+ bill and influencing broader societal norms around equality and inclusion.PAI also prioritised evidence-based advocacy as a strategic tool for influencing change. Through technical and financial support, PAI enabled activists in Uganda and South Africa to develop Spotlight Reports that documented the exclusion and rights violations faced by LGBTIQ+ communities within the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). These reports were utilised at the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF), where activists successfully amplified LGBTIQ+ concerns in discussions around global sustainable development, thereby influencing international policy dialogues and national accountability mechanisms. In addition, PAI strengthened advocacy initiatives by facilitating the development and submission of Universal Periodic Review (UPR) stakeholder reports for Egypt and Ivory Coast. These reports marked historic milestones, with Ivory Coast submitting its first LGBTIQ-specific stakeholder report to the Human Rights Council. Both reports served as critical advocacy tools to highlight systemic human rights violations and push for governmental accountability at the international level.At the regional level, PAI’s engagement in the South Africa Human Rights Activists Forum resulted in the co-creation of a shared regional advocacy strategy among Southern African activists. This collective approach enhanced collaboration across countries, promoting coordinated and sustained advocacy efforts to counter rising anti-rights movements and restrictive policies targeting LGBTIQ+ communities.Through these multifaceted initiatives, PAI directly contributed to increasing the number, quality, and effectiveness of advocacy initiatives led by grassroots organisations, CBOs, and CSOs. By building capacity, facilitating access to influential spaces, strengthening movement coordination, and promoting the use of evidence-based tools, PAI helped LGBTIQ+ advocates and organisations shape national, regional, and international policy landscapes. By centring participatory methodologies, feminist principles, and a strong Global South lens, PAI’s approach ensures that advocacy is not only sustained but also community-driven, intersectional, and transformative.

Recognising that effective legal and policy influence requires skilled advocates, evidence-based strategies, and access to the right platforms, Pan Africa ILGA (PAI) prioritised the development of strategic, human, and technical resources for LGBTI movements across Africa throughout 2024. A total of nine major capacity-building initiatives were delivered across East, West, and Southern Africa, directly reaching over 80 LGBTIQ+ activists, organisational leaders, and advocates. These initiatives enhanced the movements’ ability to engage with international and regional human rights mechanisms, frame compelling advocacy narratives, and influence decision-makers at multiple levels.Among the most impactful interventions were three Human Rights Mechanisms Trainings (HRMTs), which collectively trained more than 50 activists. These sessions deepened participants’ understanding of legal entry points, including the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR), the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), and UN Special Procedures. Participants learnt to draft communications, develop shadow reports, and engage with special rapporteurs—skills that directly translated into meaningful participation in pre-sessions at the ACHPR and other mechanisms. To further expand the leadership pipeline, 16 LGBTIQ+ organisational leaders from across the continent were brought together for a five-day leadership forum in Johannesburg. This convening strengthened organisational governance, policy engagement competencies, and collective resilience. Leaders were left with improved capacity to manage advocacy programmes, foster institutional sustainability, and align their work with broader movement goals.Evidence-based advocacy was another core pillar. PAI provided tailored technical coaching to support the development of national Spotlight Reports, which were presented at the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF). These reports elevated LGBTIQ+ priorities in the global sustainable development agenda while building the strategic communication skills of participating activists. The engagement was further reinforced through an Activists Soirée hosted by PAI in New York, offering a reflective space to sustain momentum and strengthen cross-country collaboration.Support for direct engagement with international accountability mechanisms was also deepened. PAI facilitated the development and submission of two UPR stakeholder reports for Egypt and Ivory Coast, providing technical support and financial resources to more than 20 local activists. These efforts were especially significant in Ivory Coast, where the report marked the first LGBTIQ+-specific submission to the Human Rights Council from the country. The process not only enabled activists to document and communicate rights violations but also fostered confidence in navigating global human rights systems.Cross-movement alliance-building was strengthened through PAI’s role in the Feminist Solidarity Convening in Ghana, where the Advocacy Manager led a session on using the CEDAW mechanism to advance LBQT rights. This gathering served as a critical intersectional space to expand advocacy frameworks and promote feminist-LGBTIQ+ collaboration. At the regional level, PAI contributed to the ACSE Strategy Validation Meeting, supporting the finalisation of a civil society roadmap for effective engagement with the African Commission. The outcome was a coordinated, multi-country strategy that aligned LGBTI advocacy priorities with regional human rights systems.These results reflect more than knowledge transfer—they represent the consolidation of sustainable, locally grounded advocacy infrastructure. By equipping activists and organisations with the tools, skills, and confidence to engage policy and legal systems, PAI has helped transform capacity-building from a discrete activity into a long-term investment in movement power and legal reform. These efforts continue to shift LGBTIQ+ actors from the margins to the centre of national and regional policy dialogues.
